finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: If the input file contains malicious data that includes format specifiers, such as `%n`, the `printf` function could be exploited to perform arbitrary writes.
finding.assumptions: The `buffer` is directly printed using `printf` without any sanitization. The input file is assumed to be attacker-controlled, which could contain malicious data.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that printf on line 18 uses a hard‑coded format string "Line: %s" and passes buffer only as a data argument. Since the format string is constant, any format specifiers in buffer cannot influence printf’s behavior, eliminating the described format‑string/command‑injection risk.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: If the input file contains malicious data that includes format specifiers, such as `%n`, the `fgets` function could be exploited to perform arbitrary writes.
finding.assumptions: The `buffer` is directly read using `fgets` without any sanitization. The input file is assumed to be attacker-controlled, which could contain malicious data.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the reported sink is fgets at line 16; fgets reads raw bytes and does not interpret format specifiers, so %n or other format strings cannot influence program control flow. Moreover, the buffer read by fgets is never passed to any function that could execute commands (no system(), exec*, popen(), etc.), eliminating the possibility of OS command injection. Thus there is no untrusted-to-dangerous-operation path. The claim of arbitrary writes via %n in fgets is incorrect.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: If the `searchPattern` contains malicious data that includes format specifiers, such as `%n`, the `processFile` function could be exploited to perform arbitrary writes.
finding.assumptions: The `globResult.gl_pathv[i]` is directly passed to `processFile` without any sanitization. The `searchPattern` is assumed to be attacker-controlled, which could contain malicious data.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the sink function `processFile` only performs file I/O using `fopen`, `fgets`, and `fclose`; no system call or command execution is invoked. The filename from `globResult.gl_pathv[i]` is passed directly to `fopen`, which is a safe operation for file paths. The reported trigger involving format specifiers such as `%n` is unrelated because `processFile` never uses the filename as a format string. Moreover, the source `globResult.gl_pathv[i]` is derived from `glob`, which expands a search pattern; even if the pattern were attacker‑controlled, it cannot lead to command injection because the filename is not used in a command execution context.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: If the `searchPattern` contains malicious data that includes format specifiers, such as `%n`, the `glob` function could be exploited to perform arbitrary writes.
finding.assumptions: The `searchPattern` is directly passed to `glob` without any sanitization. The `searchPattern` is assumed to be attacker-controlled, which could contain malicious data.

parsed.refutation_attempt: 1) Checked the source of `searchPattern`: it is defined in `main` on line 40 as a compile‑time constant string `"*.txt"`; therefore it is not attacker‑controlled. 2) Reviewed the `glob` call on line 27: the C library implementation performs pathname expansion only and does not interpret format specifiers such as `%n`. No format‑string or command‑injection vector exists. 3) No path from an untrusted source to a dangerous operation is present in the visible code. 4) No other checks or constant arguments affect the potential vulnerability.
